meta.region: South Asia smallholder systems: India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal (demonstration scope)
meta.status: DRAFT. Compiled by the author from widely published public smallholder guidance. NOT yet validated by a local agronomist. Every entry carries validated=false until an extension officer signs it off.

entries.title: When to plant maize
entries.keywords: when plant sow sowing planting time season kharif rabi spring monsoon winter start rains onset first rain early late date calendar
steps: Maize is grown in the monsoon (kharif), winter (rabi) and spring seasons, depending on the area. Sowing dates differ for each season and district.
For rain-fed monsoon maize, sow when the rains have set in and the soil is moist to sowing depth, not after a single early shower.
Have seed and fertilizer ready beforehand so you can sow on time. Late sowing usually lowers yield.
If you are past the usual window, ask your agriculture extension officer about a short-duration variety.
entries.caution: Sowing dates differ by district and season. Confirm local dates with your agriculture extension officer or seed supplier.
entries.source: Compiled summary of general smallholder maize guidance

entries.title: Spacing and planting depth
entries.keywords: spacing distance between rows plants depth deep seeds per hole hill population how far apart planting density ridge ridges raised bed
steps: A commonly recommended layout is about 60 to 75 cm between rows and 20 to 25 cm between plants, with one plant per hill.
Sow seed about 3 to 5 cm deep and cover it firmly with soil.
In the monsoon season, sowing on ridges or raised beds helps protect young plants from standing water.
entries.caution: Best spacing depends on the hybrid and season. Use the spacing printed on your seed packet or given by your extension officer.
entries.source: Compiled summary of general smallholder maize guidance

entries.title: Choosing maize seed
entries.keywords: best seed variety hybrid certified improved which seed buy choose early maturing drought tolerant altitude fake seed
steps: Buy certified seed from a registered agro-dealer and keep the receipt and the sealed packet label.
Choose a variety suited to your altitude and rainfall. Early-maturing varieties suit short or unreliable rains.
Ask your extension officer which varieties perform well in your area.
entries.caution: Do not buy seed from unmarked sacks or unknown sellers; it may be old, mixed or fake.
entries.source: Compiled summary of general smallholder maize guidance

entries.title: Saving and recycling seed
entries.keywords: save seed saved recycle recycled replant own seed from last harvest hybrid second generation keep seed
steps: Do not replant grain from a hybrid variety. The next generation usually gives lower and uneven yields.
Open-pollinated varieties can be saved: choose seed from healthy, well-filled cobs of good plants, dry it well, and store it in a sealed container.
Before planting saved seed, test germination on a small sample. If fewer than most seeds sprout, buy fresh seed.
entries.caution: Check on the seed packet whether the variety is a hybrid or open-pollinated.
entries.source: Compiled summary of general smallholder maize guidance

entries.title: Fertilizer at planting
entries.keywords: fertilizer basal dap npk planting apply phosphorus manure compost at planting how much fertiliser rate sowing farmyard manure fym zinc soil health card planting hole put in hole
steps: Apply a phosphorus-containing fertilizer (for example DAP or NPK) in the furrow or beside the seed row at sowing, mixed lightly with soil so seed does not touch it.
Well-rotted farmyard manure or compost improves the soil when worked in before sowing.
Rates depend on your soil. A soil test (in India, your Soil Health Card) or your extension officer can give the right amount, including whether zinc is needed.
entries.caution: Fertilizer touching the seed can burn it. Do not guess the rate.
entries.source: Compiled summary of general smallholder maize guidance

entries.title: Top-dressing with nitrogen
entries.keywords: top dress topdress topdressing nitrogen urea can calcium ammonium nitrate second fertilizer knee high when to apply fertiliser after planting
steps: Apply nitrogen fertilizer (such as urea) in split doses, commonly when plants are about knee-high and again before tasseling, after weeding.
Apply when the soil is moist. Place it a hand-width from the plant and cover it with soil.
Do not apply during a dry spell or just before very heavy rain.
entries.caution: Confirm the right amount for your soil and variety with your extension officer.
entries.source: Compiled summary of general smallholder maize guidance

entries.title: Weeding maize
entries.keywords: weed weeding weeds hoe herbicide first weeding second weeding grass competition clean field
steps: Do the first weeding about two to three weeks after sowing, and a second at about five to six weeks.
Keep the field free of weeds for roughly the first six to eight weeks. This is when weeds hurt yield most.
Weeding before top-dressing helps the maize, not the weeds, use the fertilizer.
entries.caution: Use herbicides only if registered for maize and follow the product label.
entries.source: Compiled summary of general smallholder maize guidance

entries.title: Fall armyworm in maize
entries.keywords: fall armyworm worm worms caterpillar caterpillars holes in leaves ragged leaves sawdust frass whorl eating leaves pest larvae chewed leaf damage insect
steps: Scout your field every week from when the maize emerges. Check plants in several places across the field, looking at the leaf whorl.
Signs: small clear windows on leaves, ragged holes, and sawdust-like droppings in the whorl. The larva often has an upside-down Y mark on its head.
If only a few plants are affected, crush the larvae by hand in the early morning or late afternoon. Some farmers put dry sand, soil or wood ash into the whorl.
Tell your extension officer if damage is spreading. If a pesticide is advised, use only a product registered for maize, follow the label, and wear protective clothing.
entries.caution: Early detection matters. Do not spray unregistered or leftover chemicals.
entries.source: Compiled summary of general fall armyworm management guidance

entries.title: Stem borers
entries.keywords: stem borer borers dead heart tunnel stalk holes in stem wilting central leaf dies sawdust stalk shoot fly
steps: Signs include small holes in leaves, a dead central leaf (dead heart), and tunnels inside the stalk.
After harvest, remove or destroy old stalks, which can shelter the pest between seasons.
Rotating crops and planting at the recommended time help reduce attacks. Ask your extension officer about push-pull intercropping.
entries.caution: Confirm the pest before treating. Damage can look similar to other problems.
entries.source: Compiled summary of general smallholder maize guidance

entries.title: Waterlogging in the monsoon
entries.keywords: waterlogging waterlogged standing water flood flooded heavy rain monsoon drainage drain too much water water stays in field yellow after rain
steps: Maize is sensitive to standing water, especially when young. Even a few days of waterlogging can damage the crop.
Open drainage channels so water leaves the field quickly after heavy rain.
In areas where water often stands, sow on ridges or raised beds and avoid low-lying plots for monsoon maize.
After the water drains, ask your extension officer whether extra nitrogen is advisable, since waterlogged plants often turn yellow.
entries.caution: Yellowing after heavy rain can also have other causes. An extension officer should confirm.
entries.source: Compiled summary of general smallholder maize guidance

entries.title: When to irrigate maize
entries.keywords: irrigate irrigation watering give water critical stages tasseling silking grain filling canal tubewell how often water schedule
steps: Maize needs water most at the knee-high stage, at tasseling and silking (flowering), and during grain filling.
Do not let the crop run short of water at flowering. Stress then causes the largest yield loss.
Irrigate so the soil is moist but water does not stand in the field. Furrow irrigation between ridges uses less water than flooding.
entries.caution: How often to irrigate depends on soil, season and weather. Ask your extension officer for a local schedule.
entries.source: Compiled summary of general smallholder maize guidance

entries.title: Crop rotation and intercropping
entries.keywords: rotation rotate intercrop intercropping beans legumes cowpea groundnut soil fertility mix crops what to plant after maize pulses mung moong soybean chickpea
steps: Rotate maize with legumes such as mung bean, cowpea, soybean or chickpea. Legumes add nitrogen to the soil and break pest and disease cycles.
Short legumes can be grown between maize rows if spacing allows.
Avoid growing maize on the same plot year after year.
entries.caution: Intercropping needs enough space and moisture for both crops.
entries.source: Compiled summary of general smallholder maize guidance

entries.title: Saving soil moisture
entries.keywords: keep water in field little rain hold water moisture conserve mulch mulching ridges tie ridge basin planting basins zai erosion runoff dry conserve rain harvesting
steps: Cover the soil between rows with crop residue, straw or other mulch to reduce evaporation and slow weeds.
On slopes, plant along the contour and use tied ridges or planting basins to catch rain.
Keep weeds down, because weeds use soil water that maize needs.
entries.caution: Mulch can hide pests. Check plants regularly.
entries.source: Compiled summary of general soil and water conservation guidance

entries.title: Maize under drought stress
entries.keywords: drought dry leaves rolling rolled curling wilting no rain rain stopped heat stress water stress tassel silking heat hot wind
steps: Leaf rolling in the hottest part of the day is common. If leaves stay rolled in the morning, the plants are short of water.
Remove weeds so they do not compete for the remaining water, and keep mulch on the soil.
Do not apply top-dressing fertilizer to dry soil. Wait for rain.
Ask your extension officer about drought-tolerant and early-maturing varieties for next season.
entries.caution: Water shortage or extreme heat around flowering (tasseling and silking) hurts yield the most. This is a common risk for spring maize.
entries.source: Compiled summary of general smallholder maize guidance

entries.title: Leaf colour and nutrient problems
entries.keywords: yellow leaves purple leaves leaf colour color pale light green v shaped tip yellowing nitrogen phosphorus deficiency nutrient hunger purplish white stripes white bud zinc pale bands
steps: Yellowing in a V shape starting at the leaf tip and moving along the midrib often points to nitrogen shortage, especially on older leaves.
Purplish colour on young plants often points to phosphorus shortage or cold, wet soil.
Broad whitish or pale yellow bands near the base of young leaves often point to zinc shortage, which is common in many South Asian soils.
Compare with healthy plants nearby and with other causes such as pests, disease or waterlogging, and ask your extension officer to confirm before spending on fertilizer.
entries.caution: Many problems look alike. A soil test is the reliable way to find out.
entries.source: Compiled summary of general crop nutrition guidance

entries.title: Soil testing and acid soils
entries.keywords: soil test testing acid acidic lime liming ph poor soil where to test soil sample low yield
steps: A soil test shows acidity (pH) and nutrient levels, so you apply only what the soil needs.
Ask your extension office or a registered laboratory how to take and send a sample.
If the soil is acidic, lime may be recommended along with fertilizer.
entries.caution: Apply lime and fertilizer only as the soil test report or extension officer advises.
entries.source: Compiled summary of general soil fertility guidance

entries.title: Leaf blights and rust
entries.keywords: spots on leaves leaf spot leaf blight turcicum northern blight banded sheath blight rust brown orange pustules lesions fungus fungal disease cigar shaped
steps: Turcicum (northern) leaf blight shows as long, cigar-shaped grey-green or tan lesions on the leaves. Rust shows as small raised orange-brown pustules.
Banded leaf and sheath blight, common in warm humid monsoon weather, shows as bands of bleached and dark tissue on lower leaves and sheaths.
Rotate crops, remove or bury old maize residue after harvest, and avoid very dense planting.
Ask about resistant hybrids for your area. Use a fungicide only if an extension officer recommends it.
entries.caution: Diseases are worse in warm, humid weather and where maize follows maize.
entries.source: Compiled summary of general maize disease guidance

entries.title: When to harvest maize
entries.keywords: harvest harvesting ready mature maturity when to harvest husks dry black layer cobs ripe pick
steps: Harvest when the husks have dried and the kernels are hard. A dark layer at the base of the kernel shows physiological maturity.
Harvesting promptly after the crop dries reduces losses to rain, pests, birds and mould.
Dry the cobs or grain quickly and well before storing.
entries.caution: Harvesting wet and storing it damp leads to mould and spoilage.
entries.source: Compiled summary of general smallholder maize guidance

entries.title: Drying and storing grain
entries.keywords: how to store maize storage store storing weevil weevils stored grain drying dry moisture hermetic bag pics bags large grain borer insects in store granary
steps: Dry grain until it is hard and dry. A safe moisture level for storage is about 13.5 percent, which a moisture meter from your extension officer or cooperative can check.
Clean sacks and the store first, and remove any damaged or mouldy grain before storing.
Store in hermetic (airtight) bags, such as triple-layer bags, and keep them off the bare floor and away from walls.
Check stored grain regularly for insects, heat or a musty smell.
entries.caution: Storing grain that is not fully dry is the main cause of mould and loss.
entries.source: Compiled summary of general post-harvest guidance

entries.title: Mould and aflatoxin in maize
entries.keywords: aflatoxin mould mold moldy green mouldy kernels fungus toxin unsafe to eat musty grain poison spoiled maize
steps: Mouldy grain can carry aflatoxin, a toxin that harms health and cannot be removed by cooking.
Sort out and discard discoloured, shrivelled or mouldy kernels before storing or selling. Do not feed them to people or animals.
Prevent mould by drying maize quickly and fully, storing it dry in clean airtight bags, and keeping it off the ground.
entries.caution: If grain smells musty or shows green or black mould, do not eat it. Ask your extension officer how to dispose of it.
entries.source: Compiled summary of general food safety guidance for maize

entries.title: Using pesticides safely
entries.keywords: pesticide spray sprayer chemical insecticide safe safety protective clothing registered label children storage leftover which pesticide product use
steps: Use only products registered for maize in your country and for the specific pest. Ask your extension officer or a registered agro-dealer.
Read the label and follow the instructions exactly. Do not mix your own stronger doses.
Wear protective clothing, gloves and a mask. Do not spray in strong wind or near water, and never eat or drink while spraying.
Store chemicals in their original containers, locked away from children and food.
entries.caution: Pesticide doses must come from the product label or an extension officer, not from a chat message.
entries.source: Compiled summary of general pesticide safety guidance

entries.title: Selling maize and getting a better price
entries.keywords: sell selling market marketing price buyers cooperative group sell together wait until price better bargain middleman mandi fpo farmer producer organisation trader
steps: Prices are often lowest right after harvest. If you can store grain safely, you may be able to sell later at a better price.
Selling together through a farmer group, cooperative or farmer producer organisation can help you reach buyers and negotiate.
Sell clean, dry, sorted grain, which usually earns a better price.
entries.caution: This assistant does not have live market prices. Check current prices at your local mandi or with your farmer group.
entries.source: Compiled summary of general marketing guidance
